newsitem.title: INDIA: India steel majors face dwindling profits.
newsitem.headline: India steel majors face dwindling profits.

text.p: India's biggest steel companies, hit by higher input costs, excess domestic supply and depressed world prices, face dwindling profits in fiscal 1996/97, analysts said on Wednesday.
"The steel sector is witnessing a cyclical downturn," said N. Krishnan, analyst at ICICI Securities and Finance Company Ltd (I-Sec). "There's little succour in store."

He said Tata Iron and Steel Company Ltd (TISCO), the country's largest private sector steel firm, was likely to see its net profit drop 10 percent in the current fiscal year (April-March) against a 101 percent rise in the year ago.

But state-run Steel Authority of India Ltd (SAIL), which is India's biggest steel producer with a 40 percent share in the domestic saleable steel output, is likely to post a rise of 3.0 percent in net profit this year, Krishnan said.

A Reuter poll of 14 leading securities houses released on Tuesday forecast TISCO's net profit growth to rise modestly by 12 percent to 2.25 billion rupees ($63.0 million) in the six months to September 30, 1996 -- compared to a 132 percent jump in the year-ago period.
Average net sales were projected to grow 4.1 percent to 25.98 billion rupees in the first half against a rise of 29.3 percent in the year-ago period.
The poll showed the net profit of SAIL growing 15 percent to 4.99 billion rupees in the first half and net sales rising 7.0 percent to 69.66 billion.
Analysts said a new 12.9 percent minimum alternate tax (MAT) imposed on companies in the July budget will hit TISCO and SAIL profits this year because they had been enjoying "zero-tax" status.

"We estimate tax liability of 841 million rupees and 979 million rupees in fiscal 1996/97 and 1997/98, respectively," said analysts Anand Aithal at Goldman Sachs and Sandeep Neema of Kotak Securities in a joint report.
The firm did not pay any direct taxes in the past few years because it ploughed back profits into tax-spared expansion and diversification projects.
TISCO and SAIL have also been squeezed by higher input costs caused by increases in fuel and freight that could not be fully passed on to consumers due to tougher competition.
"There's no slowdown in off-take," said Anurag Mathur, steel analyst at Peregrine Capital. "The problem is the MAT and excess supply."
Some analysts also see the prospect of cheaper imports from the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS) posing a threat to domestic steel firms.

Analysts said the big two steel majors will have to rely on improving efficiency and making more value-added products to make profits as volume growth was limited with no additions to capacity in the pipeline.
"I'm not bullish on the steel sector," said analyst Archana Choudhury at securities firm H.G. Asia. "It will not outperform the Sensex (30-share Bombay Stock Exchange index) shares."
